summary: Notes from an ISI meeting about shared interests in multimedia computer mail and agreement on some initial experiments. It is a record of the meeting rather than a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: People who wanted email to carry more than plain words met to agree on a few first trials.

questions: what was the multimedia mail meeting about
subtitle: Meeting notes on connecting computers to send mixed-type messages in 1982.

tldr.problem: Organizations developing multimedia email systems needed to share progress and agree on standards for combining images, text, and voice in electronic messages.
tldr.mechanism: Representatives from CMU, ISI, MIT, COMSAT, BBN, UCL, and SRI met at ISI in January 1982 to report their multimedia efforts and agree on initial experiments.
tldr.outcome: The group agreed to use CCITT T.4 compression for black-and-white images and planned a bitmap-text document exchange experiment, with each site developing its own image editing techniques.

today: RFC 807 is a historical record of early multimedia email research. The CCITT T.4 standard it mentions was eventually superseded by CCITT Group 3 and Group 4 fax compression methods. Modern email supports multimedia through MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), which went far beyond what these 1982 researchers envisioned.

sections.title: Early Multimedia Email Efforts
sections.content:
In January 1982, researchers from seven institutions gathered at USC Information Sciences Institute to discuss their work on multimedia email. Each organization—CMU, ISI, MIT, COMSAT, BBN, UCL, and SRI—had independently begun adding support for images, fax, and voice to their email systems.

At this time, email existed primarily for text. The challenge was that different organizations used different hardware (PERQ computers, Apollo workstations, Lisp Machines) and different encoding methods for images. Standardizing these efforts was essential for messages sent between organizations to work correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Different colleges and companies had started trying to send pictures in email, but they were all doing it differently. The leaders met up to figure out how to make them all talk to each other.

sections.title: What Each Site Was Building
sections.content:
CMU focused on voice—using an LPCM vocoder (a device that digitized speech) and an NEC board to replace it. MIT worked on storing shared message data in a centralized filing system and managing multi-recipient messages with enclosures. COMSAT had invested heavily in encoding and decoding both Rapicom fax data and bitmap (picture) data.

BBN was building a prototype system to investigate data distribution and privacy, with plans to support TCP. UCL had developed methods for encoding and decoding the Rapicom 450 fax machine and for bitmap manipulation like noise cleanup and image scaling. SRI ran three separate projects: one on mail protocols with security features, another on multimedia architecture including negotiations and multi-level security, and a third exploring natural language interfaces to data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some places were good at voice, some at pictures, and some at storing lots of messages. Each one was building their own thing, but they all needed the others to understand their formats.

sections.title: Agreements and Standards
sections.content:
The group agreed to use the CCITT T.4 recommendation for black-and-white bitmap data exchange. This was an emerging international standard for compressing fax images. The decision meant each site could focus on supporting this single format rather than translating between proprietary compression methods.

A key unresolved question was negotiation: should senders initially send only pointers to message sections and let recipients request the parts they could handle? Or should entire messages always be sent? The group decided this needed further study, as it had different implications for message relaying and interleaved media.

Another major topic was handling equipment variations. What should happen if a receiving system could not portray some data—for instance, if it lacked a voice decoder? The consensus was that the system should simply notify the user: There is some data here I can't portray and its type is X.
sections.plainLanguage: They all agreed to use the same way of squeezing picture files small (called CCITT T.4). They also agreed that if a computer couldn't display something, it should just tell the person "I don't know how to show that."

sections.title: Next Steps
sections.content:
The meeting produced several action items. Jon Postel would start a new note series for exchanging protocols, formats, algorithms, and procedures between the multimedia projects. Each site was to compare the emerging NBS Mail Standard with the RFC 759+767 approach (the existing ARPANET text mail protocol). The group scheduled a bitmap-text document exchange demonstration for April 1982 at a User Interface Meeting at CMU.

The framework agreed upon was simple: move bitmap data between computers as files using any available file transfer method, with the file structured as a complete RFC 759 document and bitmap data in the revised COMSAT Image Data Format, using either raw bitmap or CCITT Algorithm compression.
sections.plainLanguage: They agreed to share what they learned with each other through notes, and to show off a working example of sending both pictures and text together by April.
